title: How Should We Treat Status Epilepticus Stage One Plus?
content: In some patients in status epilepticus (SE), a poor response to benzodiazepine monotherapy can be predicted for a variety of reasons, including treatment delays. It has been suggested that these patients should be classified as a separate group (Stage One Plus) and treated more vigorously than current guidelines recommend. This review examines the rationale for this “more vigorous” treatment. The main factor in benzodiazepine pharmacoresistance is a reduction in synaptic GABAA receptors (GABAARs) due to seizure-induced calcium influx through NMDA receptors (NMDARs). This activates calcineurin and induces trafficking of GABAARs from synapses to perisynaptic areas or their internalization into endosomes. With fewer receptors to activate, benzodiazepines lose potency. Another factor is the seizure-induced, NMDAR-dependent inactivation of the chloride transporter KCC2, which raises intracellular chloride and reduces the ability of the remaining GABAARs to hyperpolarize neurons. Additional factors are the NMDAR-dependent increase in NMDARs and in AMPA receptors (AMPARs), causing runaway excitation which benzodiazepine monotherapy does not treat. All four mechanisms are NMDAR-dependent, and in animal models of SE, addition of a NMDAR blocker such as ketamine to benzodiazepines is far more potent than benzodiazepine monotherapy in stopping SE and preventing its long-term consequences. Other antiseizure medications can be combined with benzodiazepines to reduce seizures, but in animal models the combinations that have been tested do not approach the synergistic potency of benzodiazepine-NMDAR blocker combinations. Clinically, there are no controlled studies of the Stage One Plus concept or of treatment with benzodiazepine-NMDAR combinations in adults. However, pre-hospital ketamine given after midazolam has failed to stop SE has been used safely in uncontrolled studies. In children, a double-blind clinical trial showed that the midazolam + ketamine combination stopped convulsive SE better than midazolam + placebo (74.6% vs 20.8%, p < 0.001). In conclusion, studies of the causes and time course of benzodiazepine pharmacoresistance and controlled clinical trials of the benzodiazepine-ketamine combination as initial treatment of SE in adults are urgently needed.
